name: Prize crossword No 27,525
preamble: One solution embraces 10 others, which lack further definition

clue.text: Amaze old fellow swallowing bit of gristle

indicators.note: only a bit is wanted, so keep just the opening letter of the next word
whatever swallows something takes it inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: an old stager is a veteran, someone long experienced
the first letter of gristle

explanation.surface: An elderly man is astonished to find himself chewing on a piece of gristle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old stager' is the idiom for an experienced hand; the G slips into the middle of STAGER.
explanation.definitionFit: To stagger someone is to astonish or stun them, a common verb sense alongside reeling on unsteady legs.

clue.text: Officer's platform

blocks.note: first meaning: an elected official or military officer in ancient Rome
second meaning: a raised dais from which speeches are made

explanation.walkthrough: The possessive suggests a platform belonging to an officer, but the 's is just 'is', joining two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: In Rome a tribune was a magistrate or senior army officer, and the word also names a raised speaker's dais.

clue.text: Midnight in Georgia

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: read as mid-night: the middle of the word night, its first and last letters dropped
GA is the US postal abbreviation for the state of Georgia

explanation.surface: A late-night scene somewhere in the American South, or in the Caucasus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Midnight' reads as one word, but split it: 'mid' night is its centre letters, placed in GA. The island is defined only by the preamble's Hebrides theme.
explanation.definitionFit: Gigha is a small island off the Kintyre peninsula, counted among the Inner Hebrides of western Scotland.

clue.text: Clapton hugs politician and setter — a quack

indicators.note: to hug is to wrap your arms round, so one piece encloses the others

blocks.note: Eric Clapton, the guitarist
Member of Parliament
the setter refers to themself as I

explanation.surface: The rock guitarist embraces an MP and the crossword compiler, apparently a charlatan.
explanation.walkthrough: Eric Clapton is the British rock guitarist; the setter is always 'I'. The dash separates the definition from the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: An empiric was an old term for a practitioner relying on experience rather than training, hence a charlatan doctor.

clue.text: Flower disturbs Lettish characters

indicators.note: something disturbed is knocked out of its proper order, so the letters get rearranged

blocks.note: the letters of Lettish, an old name for Latvian

explanation.surface: A bloom somehow upsets some Latvian people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters' sounds like people but means the letters of 'Lettish', an old word for Latvian.
explanation.definitionFit: The thistle is a prickly plant with purple blooms, Scotland's national emblem, fitting a Hebridean puzzle.

clue.text: Call to account at university after reporting dining area

indicators.note: a report is something spoken, so the word is wanted for its sound
placing one thing after another sets the order of the two pieces

blocks.note: a hall is a dining room, especially in a college
a student in residence at a British university is said to be up

explanation.surface: A student is reprimanded, perhaps for misbehaving in the college refectory.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage you go up to university and are sent down when expelled; the college dining hall supplies the sound.
explanation.definitionFit: To haul someone up is to bring them before an authority for a reprimand, the idiom matching being called to account.

clue.text: Not at home and sadly is shut outside

indicators.note: things that turn out sadly go wrong, so the letters fall into a different order
one piece sits outside another, wrapping round it

blocks.note: someone not at home is out
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone finds a place closed and nobody in, a disappointing visit.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged letters SHUIST wrap round OUT after their first letter. The island needs no definition beyond the theme.
explanation.definitionFit: South Uist is a large island in the Outer Hebrides, lying between Benbecula and Eriskay.

clue.text: 49 is enough, but  …

blocks.note: 49 is one less than L, the Roman fifty, and that letter is what the clue wants; the phrase it echoes begins with a word sounding like 'L-ess'
taken as written
the ellipsis asks you to finish the thought: not enough, but more

explanation.surface: A quibble over whether forty-nine will do, trailing off unfinished.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue plays on the saying 'less is more': forty-nine is L-less by one, and the trailing dots ask for the next word. The island is defined by the theme.
explanation.definitionFit: Lismore is a long low island in Loch Linnhe near Oban, usually grouped with the Inner Hebrides of Scotland.

clue.text: Salesman getting small delight in plant

blocks.note: a commercial traveller is a travelling salesman
S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a synonym

explanation.surface: A sales rep takes a modest pleasure in a factory or some greenery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' could be a factory, but here it is the botanical sense; the S also supplies the apostrophe-s of the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Traveller's joy is the wild clematis, a climbing hedgerow species with fluffy seed heads common in Britain.

clue.text: Some of the Baggies coming back

indicators.note: only some of the letters are wanted, a run lying inside the words
coming back means travelling the other way, so the letters read right to left

blocks.note: the run of letters inside this word

explanation.surface: Some West Bromwich Albion supporters returning home; the Baggies is that football club's nickname.
explanation.walkthrough: The football nickname is a red herring; only its inner letters matter, read backwards. The theme supplies the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Eigg is one of the Small Isles of the Inner Hebrides, famous for its community buyout of the island.

clue.text: Language from rogue upset eccentric

indicators.note: an eccentric is off-centre and odd, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, though it looks like a second signal

explanation.surface: Words from a scoundrel who has upset an odd character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' wants to be the signal, but it is part of the fodder; 'eccentric' does the rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: Portuguese is the Romance tongue spoken in Portugal, Brazil and several African countries.

clue.text: Golden couple's young domestic worker

blocks.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
a synonym

explanation.surface: A celebrated couple employs a young helper at home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Golden couple' reads as a glamorous pair; split it into a chemical symbol and a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: An au pair is a young foreigner living with a family, helping with childcare and housework in exchange for board.

clue.text: Stand surety against posh church roof repairs

indicators.note: a thing under repair is taken apart and put back, so its letters are rebuilt in new order

blocks.note: V for versus
U means upper-class, as in U and non-U
a standard abbreviation
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone backs an appeal to restore the roof of a smart church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stand surety' is the definition, not part of a fundraising appeal; 'posh' as U comes from the old U and non-U classification of upper-class speech.
explanation.definitionFit: To vouch for someone is to guarantee their character or debts, exactly what a guarantor offering security does.

clue.text: Unfortunately, unable to include Tooting's follower

indicators.note: when things go unfortunately they go awry, so the letters land in a new order
to include is to take in, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written
Tooting Bec is a district and Tube station in south London, so Bec follows Tooting

explanation.surface: An apology for failing to include a south London suburb's devotee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tooting's follower' sounds like a fan of the area, but it is the word that comes after Tooting in the place name. The theme defines the island.
explanation.definitionFit: Benbecula is a flat island in the Outer Hebrides linked by causeways between North and South Uist.

clue.text: They weren't Liberals it turns out, dropping left

definitions.text: They weren't Liberals it turns out, dropping left

indicators.note: dropping something means letting it fall away, so a letter is removed
what turns out differently ends up rearranged, so the letters change order

blocks.note: taken as written
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A political verdict: these people were never Liberals, and they abandoned the left.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove one L and rearrange. The whole clue also describes New Labour supporters of Tony Blair, who moved the party rightward, the British former Prime Minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Followers of Tony Blair were Labour, not Liberal Democrats, and critics accused them of deserting the party's leftist tradition.

clue.text: Initial investigation into family line

indicators.note: the initial of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept
going into something means ending up inside it

blocks.note: the first letter of investigation
a family tree traces a line of descent

explanation.surface: The first stage of genealogical research into a family's ancestry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initial investigation' reads as a preliminary inquiry; here it is just a single letter. The island is defined by the theme.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiree is the westernmost island of the Inner Hebrides, known for sunshine, windsurfing and flat machair grassland.

clue.text: Ain't professional

blocks.note: ain't stands for 'is not'; keep the first word, and let the negative attach to the next word
with the 'not' carried over, not professional means lay, amateur

explanation.surface: A colloquial dismissal: whoever this is just isn't a pro.
explanation.walkthrough: Expand ain't to 'is not' and read 'is not professional' as 'is lay', since lay people are non-experts. The theme defines the island.
explanation.definitionFit: Islay is the southernmost island of the Inner Hebrides, renowned for its peaty single malt whisky distilleries.

clue.text: Female has lived at moonshine outlet

blocks.note: the female pronoun
to have been is to have existed or lived

explanation.surface: A woman has made her home at a place selling illicit liquor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has lived' is a verb phrase that gives the past participle of 'be'.
explanation.definitionFit: A shebeen is an unlicensed drinking den, originally Irish, selling illegally distilled spirits such as poteen.

clue.text: Over half a dozen links of forty years ago

blocks.note: one more than six
a synonym, connections

explanation.surface: More than six golf courses dating back four decades.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Links' tempts towards golf courses, but means bonds. The puzzle appeared around 2017, so forty years earlier was the 1970s.
explanation.definitionFit: Seen from about 2017, the decade four decades back is the 1970s; 'of' lets the noun phrase stand for that era.

clue.text: Father raised girl

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising something lifts it upward, so it reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: to sire is to father; a sire is a male parent
a girl's name

explanation.surface: A dad brought up his daughter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Father raised girl' reads as a parent rearing a child; instead the father is flipped upward, then a name follows. The island is defined by the theme.
explanation.definitionFit: Eriskay is a small island in the Outer Hebrides, famous for the SS Politician wreck behind Whisky Galore.

clue.text: Former City off-road vehicle to perform

blocks.note: an ex is a former partner
EC is the postcode area for the City of London
a ute is a utility vehicle, a pickup

explanation.surface: An old City financier's four-by-four is going to perform.
explanation.walkthrough: The City is London's financial district, postcode EC; a ute is Australian slang for a pickup truck.
explanation.definitionFit: To execute a manoeuvre or plan is to carry it out, a direct synonym for performing it.

clue.text: Head worried about getting stick

indicators.note: a worried thing is shaken and fretted at, so its letters are disturbed into new order

blocks.note: taken as written
re means concerning, about

explanation.surface: An anxious headteacher is concerned about being given the cane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick' looks like a noun, the cane a head might give; it is the verb meaning cling.
explanation.definitionFit: To adhere is to cling or remain fastened, the verb sense of sticking to a surface.

clue.text: Theme of Jews out West admitting identity

indicators.note: something out is gone, so one letter is removed
to admit is to let in, so a piece is placed inside

blocks.note: a synonym
W is the abbreviation for west
ID is short for identity, as on a card

explanation.surface: A topic concerning Jewish people who have moved away to the West.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Theme' is literal: this answer is the puzzle's subject, and per the preamble it contains ten islands answering other clues.
explanation.definitionFit: The puzzle's subject is this Scottish island chain, and ten other answers are its islands, defined by the preamble.

clue.text: I am nicked — no way — and charged

indicators.note: saying no to something leaves it out, so these letters are taken away

blocks.note: the contraction I'm
nicked and busted are both slang for arrested
ST, street, is a way

explanation.surface: A criminal's admission: arrested, no escape, and formally accused.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charged' looks like the police charge following the arrest; it means filled. In British slang, nicked means arrested.
explanation.definitionFit: Something imbued is saturated or filled with a quality, as a room is charged with tension.

clue.text: Block artist

blocks.note: to bar is to block
RA, Royal Academician, is a standard crossword artist

explanation.walkthrough: With no definition, both words are wordplay; the theme defines the island.
explanation.definitionFit: Barra is an island near the southern end of the Outer Hebrides, famous for its beach airport.

clue.text: Well-bred people, quiet and not from the county

blocks.note: a synonym, mild and soft
the phrase is 'county folk'; strip away the county and the people remain

explanation.surface: Genteel types, softly spoken, who are not local gentry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'County folk' is a British phrase for the landed set of a shire; the clue keeps only the people.
explanation.definitionFit: Gentlefolk is an old-fashioned term for people of good birth and refined manners, the genteel classes.

clue.text: Rich uniform covers

indicators.note: covers are the outside of a book, so only the two end letters are kept

blocks.note: the first and last letters of Rich
the first and last letters of uniform

explanation.surface: A lavish uniform conceals what lies beneath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Covers' applies to both words, taking only their outsides. The theme defines the island.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhum, now usually spelt Rum, is the largest of the Small Isles in the Inner Hebrides, a nature reserve.

clue.text: Dance and workout teens arranged

indicators.note: arranging things puts them into a new order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: split as work + out: op, short for opus, is a work, and out says it goes outside
taken as written

explanation.surface: Teenagers organise a dance and an exercise session.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Workout' looks like exercise but splits as work + out: OP goes outside the jumbled teens.
explanation.definitionFit: The one-step is a ballroom dance of the early twentieth century, a quick walking style done to ragtime.

clue.text: Turned off tragedy

indicators.note: something off is wrong or awry, so the letters are out of their proper order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone was put off by a sad play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned off' reads as a phrase meaning repelled; split it into the definition and the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To gyrate is to revolve or spin around a centre, so the past tense means rotated or spun.
